readerMoment: Has a listener inventory, a dated device baseline and the translation-versus-permission model, and suspects the router holds openings nobody chose on purpose.
outcome: Can audit the inbound openings on their own router, close the silent ones with the owner's okay, and prove a closed opening fails from both inside and outside.
coreModel: Every inbound opening on your router needs a name and a reason, and a closed opening is only closed when it provably fails from both sides.

prerequisites.idea: Router role between inside and outside

teachingShape.realTask: Audit the inbound openings on your own router and close the ones nobody chose
activate: Your listener inventory: each LAN-facing listener is something an opening could reach
Your dated baseline: every change today gets recorded there
Translation versus permission: a missing mapping is not a stated rule, so openings are checked by name
demonstrate: One worked example household router: UPnP on with two app-requested mappings, one stale manual forward, remote administration off; each finding walked to keep, close or unknown
apply: Sign in to your own router and list UPnP status, active mappings, manual forwards and WAN administration
Label each entry keep, close or unknown from your own records, asking the authorized owner about anything unfamiliar
Close the silent entries one change at a time and record each change
integrate: Prove a closed entry fails twice: the router no longer lists it, and a connection you own on cellular cannot get through
The closed list and the named keeps join the dated baseline; the boundary is now ready to build on

requiredIdeas: UPnP lets devices ask the router for mappings without a prompt; enabled UPnP plus an unrecognized mapping is silent exposure.
Every manual port forward points at one private host and needs an owner and a current reason.
Remote administration from the WAN side is itself an opening; off is the default to keep.
Closing is a deliberate change on your own authorized router: read first, change one thing at a time, record each change.
Proof has two sides: the router no longer lists the opening, and an outside attempt from a connection you own fails. One side alone is not proof.
An unfamiliar entry stays unknown until your own records or the authorized owner names it; unknown is not closed by guessing.
candidateAnalogies: Closing openings is like re-keying a house: first list every key you did not cut, then decide which doors actually need them.
visualNeeds: A worked keep/close/unknown table for the example router
A two-side proof picture: inside view versus outside attempt

deliberatelyExcluded.what: Deliberately exposing a service with a new forward or exception
deliberatelyExcluded.why: A chosen opening needs the boundary and monitoring pages first.
Your own phone on cellular is an outside attempt you fully own; a scanner service learns your address for no extra proof.

deliberatelyExcluded.what: Replacing or bridging an ISP-supplied router
deliberatelyExcluded.why: A bigger change than this page; record it as unknown and ask the provider or owner.

deliberatelyExcluded.what: Testing addresses you do not own

nextPagePressure: With silent openings closed and the keeps named, the reader can build the lab boundary and prove the lab cannot reach trusted devices.
